analysis.one_liner: Makes child care a universal entitlement for children from six weeks to school age, with fees capped at 7% of family income.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2019 with 28 House sponsors, the bill was referred to the Education and Labor Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a universal child care and early learning program run through the Department of Health and Human Services. Every child from six weeks old until school age would be entitled to a slot, with no income test, no citizenship test, and no requirement that a parent be working [S2][S3]. Families below 200% of the poverty line would pay nothing; all other families would pay on a sliding scale capped at 7% of income [S2][S3]. The federal government would pay most of the cost, with states, localities, and families covering the rest [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children — the bill would cap what any family pays for child care at 7% of income and make it free for families below twice the poverty line, and guarantee a placement for every child whose parent requests one. Child care workers would also gain: the bill requires sponsors to pay compensation set through a bargaining process with staff and family providers, and to build training and career ladders [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Every covered child — from six weeks of age until the state's compulsory school age — is entitled to a child care and early learning placement regardless of family income, disability, citizenship, or employment status [S2][S3].
Families below 200% of the poverty line pay no fee; other families pay on a sliding scale capped at 7% of income no matter how many children they enroll [S2][S3].
Programs must run a full working day (at least 10 hours) and a full calendar year, including nonstandard-hours care, so the schedule matches parents' actual work schedules [S3].
The bill requires sponsors to recognize and bargain with unions representing child care teachers and family child care providers, and to pay staff compensation meeting the bill's requirements [S3].
Children of migrant and seasonal farmworkers and Native American children get 100% federal coverage of program costs, and tribal organizations get first claim on programs on tribal land [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an open-ended appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary') for the entitlement plus $500 million a year for fiscal 2020–2030 for supporting activities. States, localities, or other sponsors cover the non-federal share — 20% of costs for low-income children and 50% for others — and can count family fees toward it [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, states, and wealthier families

drawbacks.text: The core program is an open-ended, uncapped entitlement: the bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary,' so the federal cost would depend entirely on how many families enroll, with no price tag in the bill itself [S3].

States and local sponsors must cover a non-federal share — 20% of costs for low-income children and 50% for children who are not low-income — and are barred from cutting their existing child care spending to make up the difference, which pressures state budgets [S3].

The bill imposes national program standards, a federal facilities code, union bargaining requirements, and compensation rules on providers; small home-based providers could face significant new administrative and compliance burdens even as they gain customers [S3].

Because participation is voluntary for families ('services... shall be provided only for children whose parents or legal guardians have requested the services'), families who prefer a parent at home get no equivalent benefit from the new federal spending [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: child care is one of the biggest household expenses for families with young children, and the bill both caps what families pay and guarantees a slot for every child whose parent asks for one, while raising pay and standards for child care workers. The honest cost is that the bill writes a blank check — an uncapped federal entitlement with no estimated price — and pushes a real funding share onto states, which must keep up their own child care spending to qualify. The design borrows deliberately from Head Start and the military child care program, which are existing tested models, but scaling them nationally would be a major new federal commitment.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee in June 2019, and that is where it stayed — no hearing, no vote, no floor action — until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Debra Haaland introduced the Universal Child Care and Early Learning Act on June 18, 2019, with eight original cosponsors including Reps. Lee, Norton, Raskin, Pocan, Larson, Horsford, Meng, and Sablan [S3].
The same day, the House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and Labor, the only action recorded on the bill besides its introduction [S5].
The bill gathered 27 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never advanced out of committee; the Congress ended January 3, 2021 [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Families with young children are no better off — they continue to pay whatever the child care market charges. The existing child care industry is unchanged, and no federal money was spent on the program. Members who never advanced the bill faced no vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing child care market, unchanged

for.name: Rep. Debra Haaland
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 18, 2019 and recruited eight original cosponsors.

for.name: 27 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Bobby Scott, D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 18, 2019 and took no recorded action on it — no markup, no vote, no report — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so the only recorded partisan signal is the sponsorship list.

industries.industry: Child care and early learning providers
industries.note: The bill would channel an open-ended federal entitlement through centers, family child care homes, and delegate providers — including for-profit organizations — creating a permanent, federally funded customer base for every enrolled child. At the same time it subjects providers to national standards, a federal facilities code, and union bargaining and compensation requirements.

industries.industry: Child care and early learning workers
industries.note: The bill requires compensation set through bargaining with staff and family providers, plus career ladders and training — directly targeting the low pay typical of the field, which the bill treats as necessary for quality.
They would gain a federal funding stream for an early-learning system but must cover 20–50% of costs and are barred from reducing their own child care spending to pay for it.
